item.title: Join us for Black Women's Equal Pay Day Signing Event
item.description:
Did you know that Black women, on average, earn $0.67 for every $1.00 earned by white men? The wage gap is a persistent issue that requires our collective efforts to close.

Join us on Black Women’s Equal Pay Day for networking and a public signing of the Columbus Commitment Pay Equity Pledge at the Adelphi Bank, Ohio’s first Black-owned bank. Whether you are a professional, entrepreneur, or simply interested in supporting the cause, this event welcomes everyone.

In-person space is limited.

Based on an overwhelming response, we encourage everyone to consider joining us via live stream for this incredible event! Although our in-person spots are filled, we want to ensure that everyone has the opportunity to be part of this meaningful gathering. The event will be live-streamed for those who cannot attend in person, so you can still participate and engage with us remotely. There is no need to register; everyone is welcome to join us via livestream!

 

Event Agenda

Networking: 4:30-5:30

Program and Signing: 5:30-6:00

Watch the live stream on Facebook and YouTube.

 

Amplify the Message on Black Women's Equal Pay Day!

Download our Social Media Toolkit to promote pay equity and racial justice. Inside, you'll find sample language to help you post about the wage gap experienced by Black women.

Thank you for your continued support, and we look forward to seeing you on July 27!

Questions? Please email Christina Ratleff at CLRatleff@columbus.gov

item.title: CWC April Newsletter
item.description:
Hello Spring!

With summer right around the corner already, things are warming up at the Columbus Women’s Commission. CWC is excited to recap all of the incredible things that happened over the course of the March, as well as highlight the significant events in this month’s newsletter. Read on to be informed about Columbus events, related news and policy updates on women’s issues.

Asian American, Native Hawaiian, Pacific Islander Equal Payday

“AAPI women will lose at least $240,280 over the course of a career to the pay gap.” National Women’s Law Center

Equal Pay Day for Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Women is on April 5. For every dollar paid to non-Hispanic white men, AANHPI women working full-time, year-round receive 92 cents, and all other female earners in minority groups receive about 80 cents. Many women in AANHPI communities face even larger wage gaps than these averages. This day has been set aside to not only celebrate the hard work of all AANHPI women, but to raise awareness of the need for employers to ensure that they are equally paid. Click here to read more.

Financial Literacy Month

April is National Financial Literacy Month. Its goal is to make sure that Americans have access to unbiased financial education and a thorough grasp of financial services and products. Shout out to our partner Jewish Family Services for all the work they do to promote financial literacy among Columbus residents. All Columbus residents can get free financial counselling from them presently. Click here to read more about how to gain free financial counseling.

Informed Woman Month

Statistics illustrate that despite worldwide efforts for gender equity, women are still more likely to be less informed about current events than men. April is observed as Informed Woman Month across the world, and there is no better way to kick start this month than to keep abreast of the significant things happening. To read more about Informed Women month, click here.

Lien Forgiveness Legislation

Mayor Andrew J. Ginther was joined by community leaders on April 3 to announce legislation that will forgive loans made by the city to hundreds of Columbus homeowners. Community leaders involved in this discussion included Columbus City Councilmember Shayla D. Favor and Amy Flynn, Executive Director of Modcon Living. Click here to learn more about the Lien Forgiveness Legislation.

State Of The City Address – Spotlight On The Columbus Women’s Commission

On March 21, 2023, Mayor Ginther released his state of the city address to the City of Columbus. Key themes included safety, affordability and city services.

In his address, the mayor highlighted significant achievements and key accomplishments of the Women’s Commission, and how these activities impact the city. Some of these accomplishments include the Columbus Commitment and Paid Family Leave Policy as well as the partnership between the Commission and Jewish Family Services to launch the Columbus Financial Empowerment Center. These initiatives are all-inclusive measures targeted at ensuring the economic empowerment of women, increasing worker satisfaction and retention as well as decreasing the lifetime earning gaps between men and women – a disparity we all want to see eliminated for good. To read more about the State of the City address, please click here.

Events to Check Out This April

Construction Career Expo

According to statistics, women made up 10.9 percent of the whole construction workforce in the United States in 2022. Despite the perception that the construction business is predominantly male, women have made a significant impact on the sector. Because of this, the City of Columbus is urging women more than ever to think about the rewarding careers that are available in the construction sector. Come learn everything there is to know about employment, opportunities and the advantages of working in construction with us at the Construction Career Expo Fair on April 20.

It’s Not Rocket Science: Closing the Gender and Pay Gap in STEM

On Wednesday, April 26, the Columbus Metropolitan Club will host a discussion on the need to eliminate the gender and wage gap in STEM education and jobs. Panelists of the conversation include the Columbus Women’s Commission’s very own Commissioner, Sheri Chaney Jones, who is the Founder & CEO of SureImpact as well as the Founder and President of Measurement Resources Company. Attendance requires both membership and registration. However, the event will be streamed live via this link. Lunch will also be served for those in attendance. To learn more about this event, please click here.

But You Could Have Held My Hand

This new play starts with four 10-year-olds who meet at a wedding. Little do they know this chance encounter will change their lives for decades to come. Jumping through time, the play uses dance, music and poetry to explore sexuality, gender, race and love. Check out the show times in April by clicking here.

item.title: Columbus Commitment: Action Request
item.description:
Good Afternoon Columbus Commitment Adopters,

Columbus City Council is drafting legislation to ban employers from asking job seekers to reveal their salary history. 

As you are aware, this practice can result in wage disparities and pay discrimination for women and workers of color.

Councilmember Lourdes Barroso de Padilla would like to meet with adopters of the Columbus Commitment to introduce this topic and discuss impacts of the legislation.

May you kindly respond with your availability to participate in a short briefing?

item.title: LAST CHANCE: Take the Annual Diversity Survey
item.description:
Dear Columbus Commitment Adopter,

Tomorrow is the last day to take the second annual Diversity Survey. The short-answer and multiple choice survey wants to know the resources workplaces have for diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) and how the efforts are integrated throughout the company. 

 

Take the survey now

 

The answers are compiled in aggregate and shared as a means of demonstrating Columbus’ growing dedication to having a wider range of voices and investing in DEI measures. For example, the 2021 survey results showed that 69% of the 15 respondents reported currently having a full-time employee dedicated to DEI (31% of participants have created this position in the past year). 

With regard to leadership, the survey found women make up 33% of the boards, 31% of the boards are ethnically diverse, women account for 42% of the C-suites, and 32% of respondents’ C-suites were ethnically diverse.

As the Columbus Women’s Commission continues its efforts to advance women’s well-being in our community, let’s take time to share our successes and ongoing struggles so that we can benchmark it and set goals for the next year.

Please complete the survey at https://dispatch.gannettcontests.com/Columbus-Dispatch-2022-Diversity-Survey/

Thanks for your time and consideration. We look forward to seeing this year’s results.

item.title: CWC Adopter Newsletter: April 2022
item.description:
Promoting Pay Equity

With the next phase of The Columbus Commitment Pay Equity Campaign well underway, we want to provide you all with the tools to promote pay equity within your organization and within the community. First, we would like to recognize the new adopters from the launch date, March 25, through April 19th.

Thank you for joining us in our movement and for your dedication to achieving 100% pay equity:

  1. A Kid Again
  2. Big Change Consulting
  3. Columbus Metropolitan Housing Authority
  4. The Community Builders
  5. Creative Housing Inc.
  6. The Dispatch Printing Company
  7. Finance Fund
  8. Franklinton Development Association
  9. Girls on the Run Central Ohio
  10. Habitat for Humanity - MidOhio
  11. Huckleberry House
  12. IMPACT Community Action
  13. Mango Consulting
  14. Measurement Resources Company, LLC
  15. Ohio Chapter, American Academy of Pediatrics
  16. Philanthropy Ohio
  17. Row Together, LLC
  18. Seeds Of Change
  19. SureImpact, LLC
  20. The Community Builders
  21. The Dispatch Printing Company
  22. Woda Cooper Companies, Inc.

We are thrilled for you to join us, and we are excited to provide you with additional tools to help you achieve pay equity within your organization. Pay equity is a multi-layered, decades old issue that we as a community have been trying to tackle since the start of the Women’s Commission. While we have made great strides, there’s still a long way to go.

2022 State of the Gender Pay Gap Report: Payscale

Payscale conducts an annual gender pay gap report that reveals how much women are paid compared to men while also taking into account race, job level, age, education, industry, and occupation. The gender pay gap has been slowly closing over time, but the pandemic has caused the progress to come to a screeching halt.

Click here to read the full 2022 State of the Gender Pay Gap Report.

Why Should Employers Care About the Gender Pay Gap?

Let’s go back to the basics.

Equal pay is, across the board, an economic issue for all people. Paying your employees fair and competitive wages is not only the right thing to do - it’s also beneficial for your organization.

Here are just a few reasons why it’s economically beneficial to promote equal pay within your company:

  • Higher profits - Companies with women leaders are more profitable. A worldwide study concluded that having at least 30% of women in the C-suite adds 6% to net profit margins.
  • Obtaining and retaining more talent – Demonstrating that you value your employees by providing them with meaningful work, pay advancements, and equally distributed promotions, will help your employees feel satisfied in their careers.
  • Reputation - Placing emphasis on your fair hiring practices and pay equity will help you retain good employees as well as avoid employee discrimination lawsuits. Building your brand around being a fair and equitable place to work will never hinder your company.

Click here to read more about the economic benefits of promoting equal pay.

The Importance of Pay Transparency

Equal pay is an economic issue, but it’s perpetuated by cultural and stereotypical norms. Employees have no idea if they are being compensated fairly for their work when discussions about their wages are shrouded in secrecy. Keeping employees ignorant of existing pay gaps prevents them from challenging the pay discrimination they are facing.


What is pay transparency?
In its simplest form, pay transparency is the practice of openly discussing employee salaries within a company. It’s a tool that gives employees a better understanding of how they are compensated, and it helps employees know what they need to do to reach the next level.

Pay transparency will look different for every company, but at its very basic form employers should:


5 STEPS FOR BETTER PAY TRANSPARENCY

  • Determine where your company currently falls on the pay transparency spectrum, and where you want to be. Survey managers to understand what employees want to know about their salaries.
  • Develop a pay philosophy that aligns with your talent strategy and culture. What do you value in new hires? Which behaviors do you want to incentivize?
  • Clearly define roles and responsibilities, and use market data to set salary ranges. This helps to eliminate bias and create a less subjective pay structure.
  • Conduct a payroll audit to identify and resolve salary discrepancies.
  • Train managers to have proactive salary conversations with employees. There’s no way to do this right they aren’t on board.

Watch this TEDx Talk to learn about how pay transparency can further help your company.

Occupational Segregation

Another aspect of the gender wage gap, occupational segregation, occurs when one demographic group, in this case women and women of color, are over and underrepresented among different kinds of work or jobs. For example, men in 2015 held 98% of construction jobs and only 30% of jobs in education. Stereotypes about which gender is suited for certain kinds of work promotes occupational segregation, and this is not only hindering women in the workforce but the overall growth of the economy.

While this is an issue for the entire labor force, here are a few key effects that become aggravated as a result of occupational segregation:

  • It limits the ability of companies to match skill sets with jobs, regardless of gender.
  • It depresses the labor force participation rate when workers are unwilling to take jobs in a growing sector due to perceived notions of what is “men’s work” compared to “women’s work.”
  • Occupations typically held by men are usually paid better regardless of skill or education level, and work predominantly done by women is undervalued in the labor market.
  • Half of the gender wage gap can be attributed to women working in different occupations and industries, and the negative bias surrounding these occupations.

Click here to read more on occupational segregation.

Click here to read why occupations held by women are undervalued, and why women work in these fields.

item.title: TOMORROW: Columbus Commitment campaign kick-off
item.description:
The Columbus Commitment: Advancing Pay Equity for Women in Our Community 

Friday, March 25, 2022
12 p.m. – 1 p.m.

Register

Please join the Columbus Women's Commission on Friday, March 25, 2022, and learn how to join our movement in 2022: 100 Adopters. 100 Days. 100% Committed. 

Did you know that overall, women in the United States are paid 83 cents for every dollar paid to white men?  

  • This amounts to an annual gender wage gap of $10,435. Women of color experience an even greater disparity.  
  • African American women earn 63 cents for every dollar a white man makes, while Latina women earn 57 cents. 

Pay inequality isn’t just a women’s issue, it’s a family issue and an economic issue. These lost wages mean women and their families have less money to support themselves, save and invest for the future as well as spend on goods and services. 

Paying your employees equitably is, put simply, the right thing to do – and it’s good for business. Research has shown that increasing diversity in business fosters innovation, improves the bottom line and helps with recruitment. 

In 2017, the Columbus Women’s Commission created the Columbus Commitment a voluntary, employer-led pledge to close the wage gap and achieve pay equity for working women. To-date, over 285 local employers have signed the pledge and are examining their practices to address equity. We are thrilled to reinvigorate this campaign during the month of International Women’s Day and Equal Pay Day.   

The pay equity campaign, 100 Adopters.100 Days. 100% Committed will run from March 25 through July 3rd. 

In this webinar, First Lady and Chair of the Columbus Women’s Commission, Shannon Ginther, will share about the Columbus Commitment and the short and long-term benefits of joining. A panel of commissioners and local employers will share best practices for building equitable and inclusive workplaces, and answer attendee questions. 

We invite employers to learn how to become one of the 100 new adopters in the next 100 days! 

Have questions before the webinar? Email Christina Ratleff at CLRatleff@columbus.gov.

item.title: CWC Adopter Newsletter: Equal Pay Day
item.description:
JOIN US! The Columbus Commitment: Advancing Pay Equity for Women in Our Community

Please join the Columbus Women's Commission on Friday, March 25, 2022 to learn how to join our movement in 2022: 100 Adopters. 100 Days. 100% Committed. 

Pay inequity isn’t just a women’s issue - it’s a family issue and an economic issue. These lost wages mean women and their families have less money to support themselves and to save and invest for the future, as well as to spend on goods and services. 

Paying your employees equitably is, put simply, the right thing to do – and it’s good for business. Research has shown that increasing diversity in business fosters innovation, improves the bottom line and helps with recruitment. 

In this webinar, First Lady and Chair of the Columbus Women’s Commission, Shannon Ginther, will share about the Columbus Commitment and the short- and long-term benefits of joining. A panel of commissioners and local employers will share best practices for building equitable and inclusive workplaces, and answer attendee questions. 

Click here to learn more about The Columbus Commitment Pledge.

Click here to register for the webinar.

What is Equal Pay Day?

The month of March honors the contributions and sacrifices that women have made throughout history, and includes several important dates for women. March 8th is International Women’s Day, and this year Equal Pay Day falls on March 15th. Equal Pay Day changes each year to showcase just how far women have to work in the next year to earn the same wages a man made in the previous one. Equal Pay Day for women of color falls even later in the year. Equal Pay Laws have existed since the 1960s, but women are still plagued by discrimination and unfair treatment in the workplace. Recognizing the factors that contribute to the wage gap is the first step to achieving 100% pay equity in your organization.

Understanding the Contributing Factors: National Partnership for Women and Families

It’s important to understand what contributes to the wage gap, which is present among almost all occupations and exists regardless of education level. It’s perpetrated by bias and discrimination including stereotypes about gender and work, lack of workplace support and childcare, and the devaluation of the work a woman does compared to that of a man.

Click here to compare employment and earning by occupation.

This gap in wages results in $930 billion dollars lost by women every year in the United States alone. This is not solely a women’s issue - it affects every aspect of the community. With these lost wages, women could afford:

  • More than 74 weeks of food
  • 6 months of mortgage and utilities payments
  • The ability to pay off student loan debt in less than four years
  • 13 months of child care
  • 7 months of premiums for employer-based health insurance
  • One year of tuition and fees for a 4-year public university
  • 6 years of birth control
  • 9 months of rent

These are essential factors for a high quality standard of living, and while women work hard to achieve higher statuses in their workplace, these burdens can affect every aspect of their lives. Women are overlooked for promotions at significantly higher rates than men, and the discrepancies for women of color are even higher.

Click here to read the full report.

Gender Wage Gaps Remain Wide in Year Two of the Pandemic – Institute for Women’s Policy Research

While The Equal Pay Act of 1963 was passed almost 60 years ago, we have not yet been able to close the gender wage gap due in large part to occupational segregation. This refers to the fact that women and men tend to work in different occupations, and ones that are predominately held by women are unvalued and pay substantially less than jobs predominantly held by men with the same level of skill or education.

Service jobs, held by one in four Latina/Hispanic women and one in five Black women, took the biggest hit during the pandemic. White and Asian women are more likely to work in broader occupational categories, but there are major discrepancies in pay based on gender and race across all occupations.

Click here to read the full IWPR report for the gender wage gap in 2021.

Achieving Pay Equity: Conducting Successful Pay Equity Audits

Every organization start by should determining exactly where they are in terms of pay equity. Conducting a Pay Equity Audit can help organizations discover where their inequities lie. Comparing employees that are doing “like for like” work can only be done when the information on all the employees are up to date and accurate.

Factors involved include:

  • level of experience
  • job title, department
  • hire date
  • gender
  • race
  • hours worked in past year
  • base wage salary
  • overtime pay
  • bonuses received

These factors influence the amount of pay an employee receives and are necessary to conduct a successful pay audit. Once all of this data is collected and verified, then an organization can search for outliers and identify why those individuals are receiving less pay - often due to discriminatory factors.

Click here to learn more about Pay Equity Audits, and how you can successfully conduct and analyze the data.

Next: Implementing Policy and Creating an Inclusive Workplace Culture

These steps are long-term strategies to address the inequities that women face in the workplace.  Successful implementation can reach deep into the heart of an organization and change the direction from unheard injustices to equal and fair pay practices.

DEI practices play a major role in crafting a culture within a workplace that is accepting with a level playing field for all employees. Searching for and eliminating unconscious bias will go a long way in addressing the findings of a pay equity audit.

Here are a few steps that can counter pay inequities beyond just changing pay:

  1. Address the opportunity gap. Women are readily accepted for entry level positions, but as management levels rise, the number of women in them decrease. Only 38% of management roles are held by women, and only 21% hold C-Suite roles.
    1. Why are women overlooked for higher level positions? It’s not because of their lack of experience, education, or ambition. Negative stereotypes persist in workplace cultures, and prevent women from climbing the corporate ladder.
  2. Communicate regularly with your employees about their progress, salary ranges, and policies to build trust throughout the entire organizations.
    1. Transparency in the workplace is helpful in locating inequities and is also a tactic to reduce personnel issues within a company. Pay equity is not only a legal issue - it affects a company’s ability to obtain and retain quality employees.
  3. Keep up-to-date job descriptions in order to maintain employee productivity and enhance motivation.
    1. This will also help a company obtain the right employee for each job and will provide a clear depiction of each person’s responsibilities and salary expectations.

These are only a few of the ways that pay equity can be achieved. There are a multitude of factors that contribute to this persistent issue, many of which are rooted in gender stereotypes. In order to create a culture that is accepting and inclusive, these biases need to be addressed and eliminated. Effective communication is key to establishing the base foundation for pay equity.

item.title: Join our Columbus Commitment campaign kick-off
item.description:
The Columbus Commitment: Advancing Pay Equity for Women in Our Community 

Friday, March 25, 2022
12 p.m. – 1 p.m.

Register

Please join the Columbus Women's Commission on Friday, March 25, 2022, and learn how to join our movement in 2022: 100 Adopters. 100 Days. 100% Committed. 

Did you know that overall, women in the United States are paid 83 cents for every dollar paid to white men?  

  • This amounts to an annual gender wage gap of $10,435. Women of color experience an even greater disparity.  
  • African American women earn 63 cents for every dollar a white man makes, while Latina women earn 57 cents. 

Pay inequality isn’t just a women’s issue, it’s a family issue and an economic issue. These lost wages mean women and their families have less money to support themselves, save and invest for the future as well as spend on goods and services. 

Paying your employees equitably is, put simply, the right thing to do – and it’s good for business. Research has shown that increasing diversity in business fosters innovation, improves the bottom line and helps with recruitment. 

In 2017, the Columbus Women’s Commission created the Columbus Commitment a voluntary, employer-led pledge to close the wage gap and achieve pay equity for working women. To-date, over 285 local employers have signed the pledge and are examining their practices to address equity. We are thrilled to reinvigorate this campaign during the month of International Women’s Day and Equal Pay Day.   

The pay equity campaign, 100 Adopters.100 Days. 100% Committed will run from March 25 through July 3rd. 

In this webinar, First Lady and Chair of the Columbus Women’s Commission, Shannon Ginther, will share about the Columbus Commitment and the short and long-term benefits of joining. A panel of commissioners and local employers will share best practices for building equitable and inclusive workplaces, and answer attendee questions. 

We invite employers to learn how to become one of the 100 new adopters in the next 100 days! 

Have questions before the webinar? Email Christina Ratleff at CLRatleff@columbus.gov.

item.title: CWC Adopter Newsletter
item.description:
Recognizing and honoring Black History Month

This month, we focus our efforts on supporting women of color in the workplace and raising our standards for how we craft the culture in the spaces we work. Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) practices are critically important for the stability of our economy and the well-being of women.

Black women and the wage gap – National Partnership for Women and Families

While the wage gap affects all women, a Black woman is paid an average of 20-25 cents less than a white woman working full-time, year round. These disparities are more or less drastic depending on the state, and Ohio falls around the average. The median wage for a Black woman in the United States is $43,209 per year, which is $25,000 less than the average white man makes.

Four million families are headed by a Black women, and 1 in 4 of those households lives below the poverty line. The push for increased attention to equal pay laws and the end of racial profiling is necessary now and will be until women make the same amount as a man, and are valued as equals in the workplace.

View the full report.

Women in the Workplace 2021 Report

The work burnout seen among women is significantly higher than the burnout seen in men from the last year and half of the pandemic. This burnout has been heighted by a multitude of factors.

  • Women contribute to DEI practices within their workplace in amounts higher than their male counterparts.

    • 70% of companies say that the work employees do to support DEI practices is crucial but less than 25% of companies recognize this work formally
  • 1 in 3 women have considered downshifting their career or leaving the workforce altogether
  • 4 in 10 women have considered switching their jobs or leaving their company
  • Between the entry level and the C-suite, representation for women of color drops by more than 75%

“Diversity of numbers isn’t enough on its own. Companies also need to create a culture that fully leverages the benefits of diversity – on which women, and all employees, feel comfortable bringing their unique ideas, perspectives, and experiences to the table.”

View the full report.

So how can you create a workplace culture that is diverse and accepting? Here are a few practices that you can commit to.

  1. Raise awareness. To shape workplace culture around the idea of diversity, equity and inclusion, all employees need to understand the barriers that affect women. Share data, encourage women to speak out about their experiences and invite speakers that champion DEI principals.
  1. Training is a crucial next step in making the DEI practices concrete within your company. Bias is deeply rooted. Reinforcing DEI in your workplace culture is a great way to move forward.
  2. Communication from the top-down, and the bottom-up, will help your company clearly articulate what is expected from the CEO to the managers to the employees with regard to DEI practices.

Unconscious bias test

How to confront bias without alienating people

Bias is difficult to deal with, especially in a workplace setting when relationships are professional, and marginalized communities face increased barriers to opportunities within that space. For women and people of color, being on the receiving end of bias is a hard position to be in. Weighing the cost of saying nothing can sometimes be too high, so how can you confront bias in a constructive way?

Click here to read about ways to make these uncomfortable conversations a little easier.

Call for Columbus Commitment Adopter Spotlights

The Columbus Commitment Newsletter is designed to provide resources that support and advance gender equity in the workplace to the local employers who have signed the Commitment. These resources will range from videos, to articles, to reports and engagement opportunities. We want to showcase an adopter each month who demonstrates how these practices are being utilized in the workplace setting, and to highlight that organization’s story and commitment to gender equity. Reach out to Christina Ratleff to feature your organization in an upcoming newsletter and through social media channels.  CLRatleff@columbus.gov.

Thank you for your dedication to alleviating the social and economic barriers facing women in our community.

item.title: Invitation: COVID- 19’s Economic Impact on Women Webinar
item.description:
COVID- 19’s Economic Impact on Women: A Panel Discussion on the State of Women in Columbus

Wednesday, September 29, 2021
11 a.m. – 12 p.m.

You are receiving this email as the primary point of contact in your organization for the Columbus Commitment Pay Equity Pledge.

Please share this with your internal colleagues who may have interest in this topic.

You're invited to join the Columbus Women's Commission for a two-part series, the State of Women in the Workplace, examining the pandemic’s impact on women’s workforce participation and economic security.

The COVID-19 pandemic has been devastating for women in the workplace and has substantial implications for gender equality. Within the last year nearly 3 million women in the U.S. have left the labor force. As the nation and companies look at economy recovery, what strategies are being considered to support women’s return to the workforce?

During the first webinar, Wednesday, September 29, 2021, Elyse Shaw of the Institute for Women’s Policy Research (IWPR) will provide a thorough overview of how the pandemic has affected women’s work experiences, economic security, and wellbeing. With local leaders, we will understand how women in our community have navigated the economic crisis, and what gaps persist.

This webinar is open to the public.

Part II- November- More details to come!

In the second webinar, attendees will develop an action plan with three practical actions to take in their own organizations and consider metrics to chart their progress.

item.title: Join Us for a Columbus Commitment Adopter Network Webinar
item.description:
Staying Calm and Well through the COVID-19 Storm:
Evidence-based Tactics to Build Resiliency & Wellbeing

Monday, November 16, 2020
11 a.m. – 12 p.m.

You are receiving this email as the primary point of contact in your organization for the Columbus Commitment Pay Equity Pledge.

Please share this with your internal colleagues who may have interest in this topic.

Employers have spent much of this year prioritizing protocols to protect employees and customers from COVID-19. But, how are we navigating the collective trauma that we're all living through (but experiencing very differently)? Research shows COVID-19—combined with the political tensions and racial reckoning—is leaving people more vulnerable to depression, anxiety and other mental health challenges.

As employers, in addition to focusing on employees' physical health, we have an opportunity to support their mental well-being as well. But how? What's appropriate and what's crossing a privacy line? What signs should we look for? How can we create corporate cultures that promote wellness?

You're invited to join the Columbus Women's Commission for a presentation on this timely, critical topic. After the presentation, you'll have the opportunity to join local business leaders for small-group conversations to brainstorm and discuss strategies to prioritize the mental well-being of our teams during this challenging time.

item.title: Paid Leave and Coronavirus Listening Series
item.description:
Invitation to Participate in Paid Leave and Coronavirus Listening Series

In 2018, the Columbus Women’s Commission hosted Paid Leave for the US (PL+US) in Columbus for a lunch and learn event with Columbus Commitment Adopters. They shared a wealth of information and resources for employers.  PL+US is working to better understand the paid leave needs of the business community and to develop resources to support business leaders in meeting the needs of their employees. They are looking to reach a diverse subset of employers – large and small businesses that operate all across the country.   See below for more information on how to provide your feedback and perspective to this important work. This survey is voluntary.  

As the coronavirus pandemic sweeps the globe, the paid leave needs of businesses are changing. In response, Paid Leave for the US (PL+US), Promundo and the Parental Leave Corporate Task Force are teaming up to explore how the private sector is adapting to this unprecedented moment.

Participation in the Listening Series includes completing a questionnaire via Typeform, which we anticipate will take less than 1 hour to complete. The questions focus on understanding new and existing company policies and programs with some additional US-specific questions around newly-introduced government policies. The deadline to complete the questionnaire is Friday, October 16. 

Click here for the Typeform questionnaire

The results of the questionnaire will be anonymized and compiled to produce a report that will identify how employers are currently responding to workforce paid leave needs and in what ways they require further support in the midst of the coronavirus pandemic. This critical data will inform cutting edge resources for employers to implement paid family and medical leave policies and/or programs that suit their workforce and their bottom line.

For more information, please contact Annie Sartor, Senior Director of Business Partnerships at PL+US (annie@paidleave.us).
